pedagogy.summary: The bar model (tape diagram) is the workhorse representation of the whole ratio-and-proportion strand: a ratio like 3:2 becomes 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks, and once ONE block's value is known, every ratio, sharing, scaling and percentage problem is read straight off the picture. The key idea children must build is that each block is an equal unit, and that solving is a three-move routine — draw the bars to match the relationship, find the value of one block, then read off what's asked. Teaching should establish the equal-block convention firmly, move from concrete (cubes/counters) to the drawn bar, and always draw the diagram BEFORE calculating so the structure of the problem is made visible rather than guessed from key words.
bestPractices: Establish the equal-unit convention explicitly: every block in the bars is the SAME size and stands for the same amount — the model breaks if blocks are drawn unequal.
Teach the three-move routine: (1) draw bars matching the ratio/parts, (2) find the value of one block (total ÷ number of blocks), (3) read off the required quantity — make step 2 the pivot.
Contrast part-to-part (two separate bars, e.g. 3 and 2) with part-to-whole (one bar of 5, or a whole bar split) so children pick the right layout for the question.
Progress concrete → pictorial → abstract: build the ratio with coloured cubes, then draw the labelled bar, then connect to the numeric calculation.
Label the bars fully — the total (a brace over the whole), the known value, and the '?' — so the diagram carries the problem's information.

Compare the bar model with double number lines and ratio tables on the same problem so children can say when each is most useful (bar for sharing a fixed total; double number line/table for scaling up a rate).
keyRepresentations: Part-to-part twin bars (e.g. 3 equal blocks : 2 equal blocks) with a brace showing the total
Part-to-whole single bar split into the total number of parts, one section shaded
Cubes/counters as the concrete precursor to drawn blocks
Ratio table and double number line as complementary models to contrast
One labelled block annotated with its value (the pivot of the three-move routine)
commonMisconceptions: Draws blocks of unequal size, so the model no longer represents equal units
Sets up part-to-whole when the problem is part-to-part (draws a bar of 3 for a 3:2 ratio and treats the 2 as part of it), or vice versa
Jumps to arithmetic without finding the value of one block, so the diagram is decorative rather than a solving tool
Maps the wrong quantity to the wrong bar, or forgets which bar is which after drawing

learn.summary: Teach the bar model (tape diagram) as the workhorse for ratio and proportion. A ratio like 3:2 becomes 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks; once the value of ONE block is known, every share, scaling and percentage answer is read off the picture. Build three habits: (1) draw bars matching the relationship, (2) find the value of one block (known amount ÷ number of blocks it covers — e.g. total ÷ all blocks when the total is given, or one share ÷ that share's blocks when a part is given), (3) read off what is asked — with the equal-unit convention (every block the same size) made firm first. Progress from concrete cubes/counters to a drawn, labelled bar to the numeric calculation, and always draw before calculating so problem structure is visible rather than guessed from key words. Constructing a model is the core objective; reading a prepared model is a valuable scaffold toward it.

activities.title: Build the tape diagram: draw, find one block, read off
feedback: If a learner draws blocks of unequal size, return to physical cubes: every block is one identical cube. Rebuild the diagram with equal units before drawing again — with unequal blocks you cannot say what one block is worth.

If a learner maps the total to just one bar (e.g. treats £20 as belonging only to the 3-block bar, giving £20 ÷ 3), point to the brace: it spans the WHOLE, so count every block under it (5) before dividing.

If a learner draws a reasonable diagram but guesses the shares without finding one block's value, scaffold only the pivot: 'What is one block worth?' (total ÷ number of blocks), then read the shares from that — the picture and the answer must connect.
When shares correctly add back to the total, confirm that the equal-unit structure is what made the reading possible.
activities.rationale: A representation is learned by constructing and manipulating it, not only by viewing it. Building the bars, assigning a total and deriving one-block-value turns the three-move routine into deliberate action, and the add-back check helps catch errors such as dividing the total by only one part's blocks (though it cannot catch every error, e.g. swapped shares still add back to the total).
sourceClaims: Ratio and proportion (unequal sharing, 'for every', recipes, scale) are represented with simple pictures/bars at upper KS2, drawing the model to expose problem structure before calculating.
A part-to-part relationship ('for every 1 concentrate, 4 water') is illustrated by drawing equal rectangles/parts side by side; counters or cubes are an equivalent concrete representation.
learnerActions: Given '£20 shared in the ratio 3:2', build two bars — 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks — keeping every block the same width.
Place a brace spanning all 5 blocks and label it with the total, £20.
Find the value of one block by dividing the total by the number of blocks: £20 ÷ 5 = £4.
Fill every block with £4, then read off the two shares: 3 × £4 = £12 and 2 × £4 = £8; check they add back to £20.
Toggle the same ratio between part-to-part twin bars (3 and 2) and a part-to-whole single bar of 5, and say which layout the question needs.
Repeat independently for a new problem: share £18 in the ratio 5:1 — six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.
Re-read one of your diagrams as a proportion: 'what fraction of the money is the shaded bar?' (e.g. 3 out of 5).
activities.intendedInsight: Each block is an equal unit standing for the same amount; dividing the whole by the number of blocks gives one block's value, and from that single fact every share and proportion can be read straight off the picture without a memorised rule.

activities.title: Concrete first: build the ratio with cubes, then draw it
feedback: If the drawn blocks no longer match the cube counts, re-pair each block with one cube and recount.
If a learner cannot say what one block represents, return to the cubes and name the unit aloud before drawing.
activities.rationale: A concrete-to-pictorial-to-abstract progression grounds the equal-unit convention in a manipulable object before it becomes a drawn abstraction, which guidance presents as an equivalent concrete representation of the same relationship.
sourceClaims: A part-to-part relationship ('for every 1 concentrate, 4 water') is illustrated by drawing equal rectangles/parts side by side; counters or cubes are an equivalent concrete representation.
learnerActions: Lay out coloured cubes or counters for a part-to-part ratio — e.g. 1 cube of concentrate for every 4 cubes of water.
Count the total cubes and share a given total across them so each cube (block) gets an equal value.
Redraw the same arrangement as a labelled bar diagram, matching one block to one cube.
State in words what each block stands for before doing any arithmetic.
activities.intendedInsight: The drawn block is a shorthand for an equal physical unit; moving from cubes to the drawn bar preserves the equal-unit meaning rather than inventing a new rule.

activities.title: Read a worked bar model (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner reads the brace as belonging to one bar rather than the whole, re-point to its span across all blocks.
Confirm understanding only once the learner can restate the total ÷ blocks step unprompted.
activities.rationale: Because a bar model is itself a picture, a labelled worked example with staged reveals supports interpreting the convention. This is a reading scaffold: it does not itself require the learner to build a model for a new problem, so it should lead into construction rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Study a labelled '£20 shared 3:2' diagram and, part by part, state what each feature means: a single block, the 3-section, the 2-section, the brace, any shading.
Reveal and confirm: one block = £20 ÷ 5 = £4; the 3-section = £12; the brace shows the whole = £20.
Explain back, in your own words, how the one-block value was found and how each share follows from it.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent reading of a prepared diagram — knowing what every block, brace and shaded section stands for — supports constructing your own model, which this scaffold then leads into.

activities.title: Match, read and sketch (assessment-style practice)
feedback: For a wrong match, ask which feature of the diagram (number of blocks, brace span) contradicts the chosen problem.
For an unequal-block choice, restate that every block must be the same size.
Note that selecting a correct answer here is recognition; follow it with a sketch so the learner constructs, not just identifies.
activities.rationale: Translating between representations tests well as scored items, and the included sketch step moves beyond recognition toward construction, where shaky understanding surfaces.
sourceClaims: Ratio and proportion (unequal sharing, 'for every', recipes, scale) are represented with simple pictures/bars at upper KS2, drawing the model to expose problem structure before calculating.
learnerActions: Match bar diagrams to the worded problems they represent.
Read a quantity off a labelled bar, watching for traps: a distractor assuming unequal blocks, and a distractor confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole.
Sketch the blocks for a given ratio (e.g. draw the layout for sharing a stated total in a stated ratio).
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting and translating between words and bar models — and noticing where equal-unit or part/whole choices go wrong — shows command of the representation beyond surface recognition.

activities.title: Compare the bar model with tables and double number lines
feedback: If a learner always reaches for one tool, pose a problem where the other is clearly more efficient and ask them to justify the switch.
Verbal explanation checks reasoning; pair it with building or reading a model so the visual-spatial structure is also constructed, not only described.
activities.rationale: Comparing models on the same problem lets learners articulate when each is most useful. Dialogue is useful for verbalising the reading and judging representations; it complements, rather than replaces, building and seeing the diagram.
learnerActions: Solve the same problem with a bar model and then with a ratio table or double number line.
For a fixed-total sharing problem and for a scaling-up-a-rate problem, decide which representation is most useful and say why.
Discuss with a mentor or partner: 'What does each block stand for? What is the total? Which tool fits this question best?'
activities.intendedInsight: Different representations often suit different questions — bar models are especially clear for sharing a fixed total, while tables and double number lines are often convenient for scaling a rate (though each can solve both) — and being able to choose and justify a representation shows flexible understanding.

constraints: Every block in the bars must be the same size and stand for the same amount; the model breaks if blocks are drawn unequal.
Distinguish part-to-part (two separate bars, e.g. 3 and 2) from part-to-whole (one bar of 5, or a whole split), and choose the layout the question needs.
Always draw the diagram before calculating so problem structure is made visible rather than guessed from key words.
Label the diagram fully — the total (a brace over the whole), the known value and the '?' — so it carries the problem's information.
Make 'find the value of one block' the pivot: a diagram that is drawn but never used to find one block's value is decorative, not a solving tool.
Reading a prepared model (tap-to-reveal, worked example) is a scaffold toward constructing one; it does not by itself require the learner to build a model for a new problem.
Matching and multiple-choice items assess recognition; independent construction requires the learner to draw a correct model for a new ratio.
The bar model is planar; a flat layout keeps the equal-unit comparison clear. Added depth is not needed for this representation (this is a scope note, not a claim about 3D teaching generally).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: £20 ÷ 5 = £4, shares £12 and £8 (sum £20); £18 ÷ 6 = £3, shares £15 and £3 (sum £18); proportion reading 3 out of 5 for the 3-block bar. All consistent.

The reading-scaffold activity (worked model) carries no sourceClaim: the available claim supports drawing/constructing bars to expose structure, not the reading-reveal principle, so [] is used to avoid topic-only attribution.
The assessment-style activity's attached drawing/structure claim rests on its single sketch (construction) sub-step, not on its matching/reading components; retained on that narrow basis.

The legacy entry asserted depth 'adds nothing' to a bar model; this has been softened to a scope note about keeping the layout planar for clear comparison, as catalog ratings do not establish a universal claim about 3D.

The legacy entry stated a tap-to-reveal image 'cannot' let a child build one for a new problem; retained as a scaffold limit (reading does not itself elicit construction) rather than a claim that static images cannot teach construction.

Optional interaction examples from the design notes (snapping blocks to equal width, dropping a total onto the brace, value propagating into every block at once, a part-to-part/part-to-whole toggle, a compare-view) are preserved as illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tooling.

probeDeeper: 'What is one block worth, and how did you get it?' — checks the total ÷ number-of-blocks pivot is understood, not copied.
'Show me on your diagram where the £18 is' — forces the total to be mapped to the whole (the brace), catching the map-to-one-bar error.

Counterexample: 'If I shaded one bar and asked what PROPORTION of the money it is, could you use the same diagram?' — a child who owns the model re-reads it as part-to-whole (e.g. 5 out of 6); a child who memorised 'sharing' stalls.
'Which is more useful here — this bar model or a ratio table — and why?' surfaces whether the child can judge the representation, the top response level.
assess.correctAnswer: The diagram shows a quantity of £20 shared in the ratio 3:2 — 5 equal blocks in total, each worth £20÷5 = £4, so the shares are £12 and £8. For the new one: six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws unequal blocks: makes the 5-bar blocks a different size from the 1-bar block, so the blocks no longer represent equal units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to cubes: every block is one identical cube. Rebuild the given diagram with physical equal units before drawing again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The new diagram has mismatched block sizes; the child cannot then say 'one block = £3' because the blocks aren't equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Maps the total to one bar instead of the whole: reads '£20' as belonging to the 3-block bar (or draws the £18 over only the 5-bar)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the brace: it spans the WHOLE — count every block under it (5) before dividing. Distinguish part-to-part bars from the part-to-whole brace.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 3 blocks are worth £20 (so one block = £20÷3), ignoring that the brace spans all 5 blocks

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the diagram as decorative: draws bars but never finds the value of one block, guessing shares from the numbers in the problem
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach drawing — scaffold the pivotal move only: 'what is one block worth?' (total ÷ number of blocks), then read the shares from that.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child produces a reasonable-looking diagram but reads no value off it — the picture and the answer are disconnected

responseLevels.gap: Cannot say what the given diagram shows, or draws a new one with unequal blocks, the wrong number of blocks, or the total mapped to a single bar; the picture does not represent the ratio.
responseLevels.full: Reads the given model, faithfully constructs a new one with equal blocks and the total mapped to the whole, uses one-block-value to read off any required quantity, re-reads the same diagram as part-to-part or part-to-whole as needed, and can say when a bar model beats a table or double number line.
responseLevels.partial: Reads the given diagram correctly and reproduces the layout, but treats it as illustration — does not use 'one block = total ÷ blocks' to read off a share, or mis-handles the part-to-whole reading, or needs prompting to map the total to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a bar model: two bars, one made of 3 equal blocks and one made of 2 equal blocks, with a brace over all of them labelled '£20'. First, tell me what this diagram is showing. Then draw me a new bar model for sharing £18 in the ratio 5:1.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading THEN constructing separates surface recognition from genuine command of the representation. A child who understands the model reads the total-over-blocks structure and reproduces it faithfully for the new ratio, with equal blocks and the total mapped to the whole. A child who does not either mis-reads the given bars (thinks the £20 belongs to one bar, or blocks are unequal) or, more tellingly, cannot construct the new diagram — draws unequal blocks, the wrong number of blocks, or a part-to-whole layout. The translate step (draw a new one) is where shaky understanding shows.
